title: The 2026 HIPAA Privacy Rule: what it means for health app builders | Terra
summary: The 2026 HIPAA Privacy Rule lets patients send medical records to any app. Here's what developers can build with it.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- **Your app can receive medical records.** If a provider can send records to an app, it has to send them to whichever app the patient picks.
- **Providers can't block you or bill your users.** No refusing an app over privacy worries, no fees for access through an app, and 15 days to respond where it used to be 30.
- **You're not the hospital's vendor.** An app the patient chose isn't a business associate, so you don't need an agreement with every provider.
- **The interesting part is the combination.** Lab results, diagnoses and prescriptions next to sleep, activity and heart rate, in one product.
- **You have until July 19, 2027.** The rule takes effect on January 19, 2027, and providers have to comply six months later.
- **Outside HIPAA doesn't mean no rules.** The FTC Act and state privacy laws still apply. And users will pick the apps they trust.


## What actually changed


The rule has a long name: "HIPAA Privacy Rule: Changes to Support Coordinated Care and Individual Engagement and Reduce Regulatory Burdens." It's 363 pages, and you can ignore most of them. The part that matters for apps is the individual right of access, which is a patient's right to get their own records.


Before Under the final rule


Time to respond to a records request 30 days, plus one 30-day extension 15 calendar days, plus one 30-day extension


Getting records through an app Addressed in guidance A stated part of the right of access, when the provider can produce the data in that form


Refusing an app on privacy grounds Barred by HHS guidance Barred in the rule itself


Fees for electronic access Reasonable, cost-based fee Free through a personal health app or other automated online method


Fee transparency No posting requirement Fee schedules posted online, with advance notice of fees


Identity checks Left to the provider Cannot unreasonably burden the person asking


Privacy notice acknowledgment Providers had to seek a signed acknowledgment Requirement removed


### The dates


Date What happens


January 2021 HHS proposes the changes


November 16, 2026 Final rule announced


November 19, 2026 Published in the Federal Register


January 19, 2027 Rule takes effect


July 19, 2027 Providers and health plans must comply


Until July 2027, a provider can still take 30 days and still charge for electronic copies. So nothing changes overnight. You have about eight months to get ready.


### What didn't make it in


The final rule is smaller than what was proposed in 2021. Lawyers who've read it call it an incremental adjustment, and several proposed changes were dropped. It also leaves the HIPAA Security Rule alone. There's a separate proposal to overhaul that one, now expected around July 2027.


## The personal health app right


This is the first time the Privacy Rule has defined a "personal health application." That sounds like a technicality, but it isn't. Before, the idea that patients could send records to apps lived in guidance documents. Now it's in the rule.


### What a patient can do


A patient can ask a provider or health plan for an electronic copy of their records through an app. If the provider can produce the data in that form, it has to. Formats that other laws already require, like standardized APIs, count as producible. So in practice this points at providers whose record systems already have a patient-facing API.


The definition of the record is broad. Clinical data and billing data both count, and it covers labs and radiology practices, not just the doctor's office.


### What a provider can't do anymore


- **Refuse your app.** Worries about what the app will do with the data aren't grounds for saying no.
- **Charge for it.** Access through a personal health app is free.
- **Stall.** The deadline is 15 calendar days, and going back and forth with the patient about the request doesn't stop the clock.
- **Add hoops.** No required forms, and no identity checks that make it unreasonably hard to ask.


### What counts as a personal health app


The test is who the app works for. If a person picks it and uses it for themselves, it qualifies. If it's run mainly for some other organization, it doesn't. The example HHS gives is a clinical trial app run for the trial sponsor.


One line here matters more than the rest if you're a developer. An app chosen by the individual is not a business associate of the provider. You're the patient's agent, not the hospital's vendor. That's what makes the whole thing work. It's also what creates the gap we'll get to below.


## What you can build now


Three things used to keep clinical data out of consumer products. Providers could say no, they could charge per record, and they could take a month. For apps that patients choose, all three are gone.


### Two kinds of data


Source Examples How it reaches your app


Providers and health plans Lab results, diagnoses, medications, clinical and billing records Patient-directed access under the new rule


Wearables and sensors Sleep, activity, heart rate, HRV, workouts Device APIs, or one integration through[Terra](https://tryterra.co/)


A lot of health apps only have the second row. The first row is what a doctor sees. If you have both, you can answer questions that neither one answers alone.


One caveat. Wearables don't all measure the same thing the same way. We've found thatHRV isn't comparable across devices and thatsleep tracking varies a lot by brand . So device data needs normalizing before you put it next to a lab result.


### Six things worth building


1. **Biomarkers in context.** Show a cholesterol or HbA1c result next to months of activity and sleep. What changed in someone's life between two blood tests?
2. **Coaching that knows the medical picture.** A training or nutrition plan that knows about a diagnosis or a prescription is safer and more useful than one that depends on what the user remembers to type in.
3. **AI assistants with the full record.** AnAI assistant that has both lab history and wearable trends gives better answers than one that has only half.
4. **Chronic condition programs.** For diabetes, hypertension or cardiac rehab, the clinical record gives you the baseline and the device tells you what happened in the months between appointments.
5. **Onboarding without the questionnaire.** Nobody likes a long intake form. A records connection can replace it, and the data comes straight from the source.
6. **Research that patients opt into.** Users can contribute clinical and wearable data to a study they choose. One catch: the app has to work for the user first. If it's run mainly for a study sponsor, it falls outside the definition.


### Why the economics change


- **No access fees.** Providers can't charge your users for electronic access through an app.
- **A 15-day ceiling.** You can design an onboarding flow around a wait that has an upper bound.
- **No provider-by-provider agreements.** A patient-chosen app isn't a business associate, so you're not signing one with every hospital your users go to.
- **Standard formats count.** If another law already makes a provider offer a standardized API, that format counts as producible. In the US, that means the FHIR-based patient access APIs that federal interoperability rules already require of certified record systems.


### What it doesn't fix


- **Capability.** The right only applies where a provider can actually produce the data that way. A small practice with no patient-facing API may be out of reach.
- **Plumbing.** The rule gives your users a right. It doesn't connect you to anything. You still have to integrate with each record system's API, directly or through an aggregator.
- **Timing.** Until July 19, 2027, providers can still take 30 days and still charge.


## Where HIPAA stops


HIPAA protects data based on who holds it, not what it is. It covers healthcare providers, health plans and the vendors working for them. It doesn't cover most consumer apps, and it doesn't cover wearable companies.


The new rule doesn't change that. It makes it easier to get records out of a HIPAA-covered system. It doesn't extend HIPAA to wherever they end up. HHS says this plainly in itsexisting guidance : once an app that isn't a covered entity or business associate receives health information at the individual's direction, HIPAA no longer protects it.


### Same data, different protection


Data Who holds it Covered by HIPAA?


Lab results in your hospital's patient portal The hospital Yes


The same lab results after you send them to an app you chose The app developer No


Heart rate and sleep from your watch or ring The wearable company No


An app your hospital or insurer provides to you A vendor working for the hospital or insurer Yes


The third row is the one that surprises people. Wearable data is obviously health data, and HIPAA has never covered it unless a provider or health plan is involved. The EU went a different way: theData Act now gives users a legal right to that data.


### So what does apply?


Outside HIPAA, three things protect health data in the US.


- **The FTC Act.** The FTC can go after unfair or deceptive practices. If an app says it won't sell your data and then sells it, that's the FTC's job.
- **The Health Breach Notification Rule.** This is an FTC rule that makes certain non-HIPAA companies notify people after a breach. It reaches fewer health apps than it did a year ago. On September 9, 2026, the FTC withdrew the 2021 policy statement that had applied it broadly to health apps and connected devices.One legal analysis concludes that sharing data without authorization no longer triggers a notice duty by itself.
- **State law.** More and more states have privacy laws that cover consumer health data. Washington's My Health My Data Act is the best known. How protected you are depends on where you live.


### Why the timing is interesting


Look at the two changes together. In September, the FTC stepped back from its broadest reading of the breach rules for health apps outside HIPAA. In November, a federal rule made it easier and cheaper to send clinical records to those same apps.


Neither is a problem by itself. But together they put more weight on two things: what users choose, and how the apps they choose behave.


## What your users will ask


The rule gives users a right. It doesn't give them a reason to pick your app. Once records leave the provider, your policy is the only thing protecting them, and the careful users will check. So treat their questions as a spec.


What a user will ask What you need to have


Who's behind this app? A plain statement of who you are, and whether you work for a provider or for the user


Do you share or sell my data? No third-party sharing without clear consent, and a policy that says so on one screen


Can I delete everything? One deletion route that removes clinical and wearable data together


Why do you need all of it? Scoped requests. Ask for lab results, not the whole billing history


What happens if there's a breach? A notification process you'd be comfortable describing in public


Connecting medical records is the moment someone decides whether they trust you. Good answers to these five questions are how you earn it.


## How to build for it


Getting access is the easy part now. What you do with it decides whether users, providers and regulators trust you.


### Figure out which side of the line you're on


The same app can be inside or outside HIPAA depending on who it's working for.


Your situation Your likely status What governs you


Users choose your app and connect their own records Not a business associate FTC Act, state privacy laws, your own policy


A provider or health plan offers your app to its patients Business associate HIPAA, under a business associate agreement


You do both Both, for different data flows Both sets of rules, kept separate


Check this with a lawyer before you launch. It determines your contracts, your breach obligations and what you're allowed to do with the data.


### Build as if HIPAA applied anyway


Being outside HIPAA isn't the same as being unregulated. And after a breach, no user is going to care about the distinction. Four habits hold up under any set of rules.


- **Ask for the minimum.** Only request the record types your feature needs.
- **Make sharing explicit.** Don't share with third parties unless the user clearly agreed to it.
- **Make deletion real.** One route that removes clinical and wearable data together.
- **Keep track of where data came from.** Know what came from a provider and what came from a device. The rules for each can be different.


### What to do before July 2027


1. **Pick the records you actually need.** Start from the feature, not from everything you could get.
2. **Map each data flow to a legal status.** Work out with a lawyer where you're a patient's chosen app and where you're a provider's vendor.
3. **Get the wearable side working now.** It doesn't depend on the rule, so it can be in production before clinical access opens up.
4. **Build consent, deletion and provenance once.** Design them to cover both kinds of data from the start.
5. **Pilot with providers that already have an API.** Plenty do. Access just gets faster and free on the compliance date.


### The wearable half is the part we can help with


If you want clinical and wearable data in one product, you have two integration problems. The new rule makes the first one easier. The second one is what we do.


Terra isone API for wearable and sensor data acrosshundreds of sources . You get everything in one schema, whatever device it came from. We're SOC 2 Type II audited, we act as a processor under GDPR and UK GDPR, and we sign a HIPAA business associate agreement if you need one. The details are in ourdata residency guide .


So you can spend your time on the clinical connection and the product on top of it, and not on maintaining a pile of device integrations. And if you're curious how wearable data behaves in the real world, that's whatTerra Research is for.
